claims.text: Single-phase BCC NbTaTiV exhibits unusual elevated-temperature deformation behavior.
Inherent solid-solution lattice distortions promote a high density of edge dislocations in the target RHEA.
Edge dislocations can dominate plastic deformation in BCC refractory high-entropy alloys.
Elevated-temperature thermal activation causes edge dislocations to undergo super-jogging.
Thermal super-jogs pin edge dislocations and hinder their subsequent glide.
Super-jog-mediated resistance compensates for ordinary thermal softening.
The proposed edge-dislocation super-jog mechanism produces an intermediate-temperature yield-strength plateau.
NbTaTiZrV0.5 exhibits nearly temperature-independent strength over approximately 673–1073 K, including a reported platform at 873–1073 K.
The homogenized NbTaTiV-type target alloy will exhibit a near temperature-independent yield strength over approximately 673–1073 K.
Conventional BCC pure metals and dilute alloys are controlled by screw-dislocation motion through thermally activated double-kink nucleation.
Conventional alloys generally soften as temperature increases because dislocation motion becomes easier.
The target RHEA has temperature-dependent elastic anisotropic deformation and distinctive thermoelastic behavior.
The super-jog mechanism is responsible for the target alloy's distinctive thermoelastic behavior.
The yield-strength plateau should persist under both static and dynamic loading if edge-dislocation super-jogging is dominant.
Nanoindentation and conventional uniaxial creep tests can produce substantially different creep data because their stress states differ.
TEM and neutron diffraction can identify whether edge or screw dislocations predominate during deformation.
High-temperature homogenization removes segregation while preserving a uniform, precipitate-free, single-phase BCC state.
Intentionally retained microsegregation favors conventional rather than edge-dominated dislocation behavior.
The proposed mechanism applies above approximately 673 K but below the temperature at which diffusion-controlled creep dominates.
